raw_response:
I'm 45 years old, and I've been farming my land in Quzhou County since I was twenty. I only went to primary school, so I don't read those agricultural books or calculate fancy formulas. What I know comes from working this soil every year, watching my neighbors, and remembering what went wrong and what went right.

I have six and a half mu. Every year I plant winter wheat and summer maize on all of it. That's what my father did, that's what everyone in my village does, and I'm not about to change it now. I thought about cotton because my cousin talks about it sometimes, but cotton needs too much spraying and last year the cotton price dropped — my cousin barely broke even. Wheat and maize are safe. Even if one price is down, the other is usually okay, and I always have flour and corn at home for my family.

For wheat, I plant in October after rotary tilling the field. I buy improved wheat seed from the shop in town — not the old traditional kind my grandfather used, but not the most expensive either. The improved variety grows strong and doesn't fall over in wind. At planting I put down one bag of compound fertilizer per mu, about 50 jin, and then when the wheat turns a bit yellow at jointing in spring, I topdress with urea. Altogether that's about 15 kg of nitrogen per mu. My neighbor Lao Li tried saving money on fertilizer last year and his wheat was thin and short — he regretted it. I won't make that mistake. Better to spend a bit more than risk losing half my crop. I also put some phosphate and potash, about 6–7 kg each per mu, because the soil has gotten tired after so many years.

I irrigate the wheat three times: once in winter so the cold doesn't kill it, once at jointing when it needs to grow fast, and once when the grain is filling. Water costs money — every time I pump it costs me — but dry wheat is useless. For pests and weeds, I spray three times: herbicide early, insecticide when I see aphids, and fungicide if rust looks like it might come. Last year I skipped the fungicide and regretted it.

After I cut wheat in early June, I have no time to waste. I plant maize the next day or two into the stubble — no time to plow, so we no-till plant. I use hybrid maize seed, usually whatever the dealer recommends like Nongda 372. It grows fast and the ears are big. I put compound fertilizer down with the seed and then add urea when the maize is knee-high. That's about 13 kg nitrogen per mu, plus some phosphate and potash. Maize doesn't need as much water as wheat, but if the summer is hot and dry I irrigate twice — once when it's tasseling and once when the ears are filling. I spray twice for maize: herbicide once and insecticide once for the corn borer. That's what everyone around here does, and it works.

I expect about 450 kg per mu of wheat and 500 kg per mu of maize. Two years ago I got nearly 480 kg of wheat because the spring rains were good, but last year was dry and I only got about 400. This year the soil feels moist when I dig, so I think 450 is fair. If everything goes normal, I'll keep enough grain for my family and sell the rest to pay for inputs and my daughter's schooling. That's my plan.
